content: Rats that were fed diets containing acrylamide at concentrations of 10, 50, 100, or 300 ppm showed no observable effects at the 10and 50-ppm levels. However, diets with 100 ppm and 300 ppm of acrylamide caused growth retardation within 6 weeks and 4 weeks, respectively. Fullerton and Barnes investigated the effects of acrylamide on 6to 8-week-old male albino rats. These animals were fed diets containing 100, 200, 300, or 400 ppm of acrylamide, which corresponded to daily intakes of approximately 6-9, 10-14, 15-18, or 20-30 mg/kg, respectively. Control rats were given a similar diet without acrylamide. Rats consuming acrylamide diets developed mild leg weakness as follows: at 400 ppm after 3 weeks, at 300 ppm after 4 weeks, at 200 ppm after 12 weeks, and at 100 ppm after 40 weeks. Severe leg weakness developed in all groups except those on the 100-ppm diet. The mild leg weakness observed at week 40 in the 100-ppm group did not progress during the remaining 8 weeks of the study. At necropsy, the only macroscopic findings were wasting of the hindlimb musculature and distended urinary bladders in all affected rats. Microscopic examination revealed extensive degeneration of axons and myelin sheaths in the sciatic, tibial, median, and ulnar nerves of all clinically affected animals. No abnormalities were observed in the kidney, spleen, pancreas, adrenal glands, lungs, brain, or spinal cord tissues. McCollister et al. studied the effects of low concentrations of acrylamide in the diet. Groups of 10 male and 10 female 8-week-old Dow Wistar rats were fed diets containing 3, 9, or 30 ppm acrylamide for 90 days, after which they were euthanized and necropsied. Based on assessments of appearance, behavior, growth, mortality, organ weights, and microscopic tissue examination, no adverse effects were observed in either male or female rats. Additionally, no signs of neurotoxicity were observed in two other groups of animals maintained on diets containing 70 or 110 ppm acrylamide for 189 days. In the same experiment, McCollister et al. also examined the effects of high dietary concentrations of acrylamide. Rats fed a 300-ppm acrylamide diet began to lose control of their hindquarters after 21 days, and by day 42, all 10 males and 6 of 10 females had died. Rats on a 400-ppm acrylamide diet exhibited hindquarter control loss after 14 days. Over the course of the study, affected animals showed progressive hindlimb weakness, which advanced at variable rates to complete hindlimb paralysis. Severe muscle atrophy of the thighs and legs was observed in paralyzed animals, and some also exhibited forelimb weakness. Vocalizations became coarse in some cases, suggesting possible involvement of the laryngeal nerves. Marked improvement was noted when affected animals were returned to a normal diet, with hindlimb strength recovering within 2-3 weeks, although complete recovery took several months and was dependent on the severity of the initial involvement. Microscopic examination of nerves revealed degeneration of axons and myelin sheaths in all four limbs, with evidence of axon loss in the distal portions of the tibial nerve fibers. Muscle atrophy was grossly evident in nearly all caudal limb muscles but was most pronounced microscopically in the digital muscles. Suzuki and Pfaff studied the effects of acrylamide in white Osborne-Mendel strain suckling and adult rats. One group consisted of 30 suckling rats (1-day-old, weighing 5-8 g), and the other included 28 adult rats (weighing 150-300 g). The animals received intraperitoneal injections of 50 mg/kg acrylamide in saline three times a week for up to 18 injections, with two additional adult rats receiving a total of 26 injections. Control animals were injected with saline only. Acrylamide-injected animals exhibited slowed movement. In suckling rats, slight hindlimb weakness became noticeable after five or six injections and progressed until the animals could no longer stand. In contrast, adult rats did not show changes in body weight. Hindlimb weakness became apparent after 7-8 injections and progressed to complete paralysis after 15-17 injections, accompanied by prominent hindlimb muscle wasting. Some adult rats also exhibited forelimb weakness. In animals where acrylamide treatment was terminated after the 16th injection, extremity weakness persisted for about 1 month, whereas in those receiving 26 injections, it persisted for about 2 months. At autopsy, animals with clinical signs of neuropathy showed prominent distension of the urinary bladder, while other organs were congested but otherwise normal. Electron microscopy revealed that the most common feature in suckling rats given nine injections of acrylamide was axons filled with fine filaments. Few changes were noted in adult rats euthanized after 10 or 12 injections. Many axons in the sciatic nerve were filled with neurofilaments, but the myelin sheaths appeared normal. In adult rats receiving 15-18 injections, axonal and myelin sheath degeneration was observed. Sciatic nerves and their branches in adult rats that had received 26 injections contained numerous Schwann cells and macrophages with many myelin figures and fat droplets but very few myelinated fibers. Microscopic examination of nerves from adult rats euthanized 20 or 30 days after the last injection showed numerous axonal sprouts growing within Schwann cells. Suzuki and Pfaff concluded that the peripheral nerves of suckling rats were more susceptible to acrylamide than those of adults. Degenerative changes in sciatic nerve axons, which were only seen in adult rats at advanced stages of neuropathy, were frequently observed in suckling rats at the onset of paralysis. The authors suggested that the higher susceptibility of suckling rats might be due to the incomplete development of the barrier system in peripheral nerves.
